title: Week 21 Mastery Quiz — Land-Based Empires, Diversity & State Capacity

questions.prompt: Which explanation best avoids technological determinism when studying early-modern land empires?
choices: Firearms automatically created centralized empires.
Military technology mattered, but state success also depended on revenue, administration, logistics, legitimacy, infrastructure, local elites, and political conditions.
Gunpowder had no historical importance.
All empires adopted firearms in the same way.
questions.explanation: Military technology must be analyzed within fiscal, administrative, political, and social systems.

questions.prompt: Why did large empires often govern through local elites or intermediaries?
choices: Central rulers preferred having no authority.
Large territories exceeded the information, personnel, and coercive capacity of the center, so rulers often relied on negotiated relationships with local powerholders.
Local elites were always more powerful than emperors.
Indirect rule guaranteed equal treatment.
questions.explanation: Layered governance can be a strategic response to scale and limited central capacity.

questions.prompt: Which statement best characterizes imperial tolerance or communal autonomy?
choices: It always meant modern equality and religious freedom.
It could protect or recognize some communities while remaining selective, unequal, conditional, and connected to taxation or political strategy.
It meant the state had no religious identity.
It eliminated coercion.
questions.explanation: Historical accommodation must be analyzed through rights, obligations, exclusions, enforcement, and political purpose.

questions.prompt: A central tax register lists the amount owed by a province. What can it establish most safely?
choices: The exact amount collected and delivered to the treasury.
An official assessment or administrative claim; actual collection, local burden, evasion, negotiation, and transfer require corroborating evidence.
That all taxpayers were treated equally.
That local intermediaries had no influence.
questions.explanation: Administrative records show intention and accounting structures, not necessarily implementation.

questions.prompt: Which evidence set would best test whether an empire exercised strong control in a frontier region?
choices: A court portrait alone.
Administrative records, local petitions, tax or military evidence, legal orders, settlement data, and regional accounts compared across time.
A modern political map only.
An imperial title claiming universal rule.
questions.explanation: Frontier control must be reconstructed through multiple kinds of implementation evidence.

questions.prompt: What can an imperial palace, mosque, portrait, seal, or ceremony reveal most directly?
choices: How every subject experienced imperial rule.
How rulers or patrons represented legitimacy, hierarchy, authority, prosperity, religion, or dynastic identity to intended audiences.
Exact tax collection rates.
That political claims were universally accepted.
questions.explanation: Court and monumental evidence is powerful for representation and legitimacy claims but requires corroboration for actual control.

questions.prompt: Why is the label “gunpowder empire” useful but limited?
choices: It explains every feature of Ottoman, Safavid, and Mughal governance.
It highlights the military importance of firearms and artillery but can obscure differences in administration, finance, legitimacy, religion, geography, and local institutions.
It applies equally well to every state from 1450–1750.
It proves technology caused imperial expansion by itself.
questions.explanation: Analytical labels can reveal one pattern while hiding other causes and differences.

questions.prompt: Which interpretation of the Ottoman devshirme system is strongest?
choices: It can be understood only as voluntary social mobility.
It should be analyzed as a coercive state levy that also created pathways into military and administrative service for some recruits; experiences and outcomes varied.
It proves all Christian subjects were treated identically.
It was the same as the millet system.
questions.explanation: A balanced analysis preserves coercion while recognizing the institutional roles and varied outcomes associated with the system.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest way to compare a Mughal court image with a revenue record?
choices: Assume the image is propaganda and therefore useless.
Treat each as evidence produced for different purposes, compare their claims about authority, and use tensions between representation and administration analytically.
Use whichever source presents the empire more favorably.
Assume both describe the same audience and purpose.
questions.explanation: Different source genres reveal different dimensions of power and should be compared rather than ranked automatically.

questions.prompt: Which synthesis best answers how large empires governed religious, linguistic, and ethnic diversity?
choices: They relied only on coercion.

They combined military force, taxation, legitimacy, religious policy, administrative systems, local intermediaries, negotiated autonomy, and selective coercion in different proportions across regions and periods.
They granted equal rights to all communities.
Imperial diversity had little effect on governance.
questions.explanation: Diverse empires required layered, variable strategies rather than one universal model.

shortResponse.prompt: Using at least three specific pieces of evidence from at least three source categories and at least two empires, explain how large land-based empires governed diversity without unlimited resources. Include one example of negotiation or local autonomy, one example of coercion or extraction, and one limitation in the evidence.
shortResponse.exemplar: Full-credit work makes a defensible comparative claim, explains how central institutions and local intermediaries interacted, uses multiple source categories, preserves differences among empires, and identifies an evidentiary or category limitation.
